hints: Decide which beaker is the standard hydrogen electrode by looking for the gas inlet tube and bubbles around the electrode.
Recall the three standard conditions needed for the hydrogen half-cell: gas pressure, ion concentration and type of electrode.
Think about why the Fe half-cell needs an inert metal electrode and what two ions must both be present at 1 mol dm-3, plus how ions connect the two beakers.
walkthrough:
Spot the hydrogen electrode on the left**
You can see gas A bubbling in around electrode B in solution C. That is the classic picture of the standard hydrogen electrode. The gas must be hydrogen, $\text{H}_{2}$, at the standard pressure of 1 atm. The electrode B cannot react itself, so it is inert platinum which just conducts electrons.

Add the standard acid solution**
For the hydrogen electrode to work, solution C must supply $\text{H}^{+}$(aq) at standard concentration, 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. In practice this is 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{HCl}$ or any strong acid giving 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^{+}$.

Build the iron half-cell on the right**
The right hand side is the $\text{Fe}^{3+}$(aq)/$\text{Fe}^{2+}$(aq) half-cell. Because both oxidised and reduced species are ions in solution, you again need an inert platinum electrode E to make electrical contact. Solution F must contain both ions at standard concentration, 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.

Link the beakers without mixing**
Tube D dips into both solutions. It is the salt bridge, filled with an inert electrolyte such as $\text{KNO}_{3}$(aq) or $\text{NH}_{4}\text{NO}_{3}$(aq). It completes the circuit by allowing ions to move while keeping the two solutions separate.

Final answer: A: $\text{H}_{2}$ gas at 1 atm
B: platinum electrode
C: 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^{+}$(aq), e.g. HCl
D: salt bridge, e.g. $\text{KNO}_{3}$(aq)
E: platinum electrode
F: 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Fe}^{2+}$(aq) and 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Fe}^{3+}$(aq)

hints: Compare $E^{\ominus}$ for $\text{Fe}^{3+}$/$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ (+0.77 V) with $E^{\ominus}$ for $\text{H}^{+}$/$\text{H}_{2}$ (0.00 V) to decide which half-cell gains electrons.
walkthrough:
Pick the stronger oxidising agent**
Look up the values. $E^{\ominus}(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77$ V, while $E^{\ominus}(\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_{2}) = 0.00$ V. The more positive half-cell, the iron half-cell on the right, will be reduced, so it is the positive electrode.

Follow the electrons**
Electrons are released by oxidation at the negative hydrogen electrode on the left: $\text{H}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{H}^{+} + 2e^{-}$. They travel through the wire and voltmeter to the positive electrode on the right where $\text{Fe}^{3+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}$ occurs. On this diagram that is a clockwise flow in the outer loop.
Final answer: Positive electrode is Pt on RHS ($\text{Fe}^{3+}$/$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ electrode) and electrons flow in external circuit from LHS to RHS, clockwise.

hints: Write down the two $E^{\ominus}$ values from the Data Booklet and identify the more positive half-cell as the one that is reduced.
walkthrough:
Subtract the right way round**
Think of cell potential as the driving force from the difference. $E^{\ominus}(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77$ V and $E^{\ominus}(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}) = +0.34$ V. The iron half-cell is more positive, so it is reduced while copper is oxidised.
$$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode}$$
$$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 0.77 - 0.34 = +0.43 \text{ V}$$

hints: Write the reduction equilibrium for the nickel electrode, $\text{Ni}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ni}$, and apply Le Chatelier when $[\text{Ni}^{2+}]$ falls.
walkthrough:
See the equilibrium behind the voltage**
Picture the surface: $\text{Ni}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ni(s)}$. The electrode potential reflects how strongly this equilibrium lies to the right.
Step 2 is built into this thinking: if you lower $[\text{Ni}^{2+}]$, Le Chatelier tells you the system opposes the change by shifting left to make more $\text{Ni}^{2+}$. Reduction becomes less favourable, electrons are given out more easily, so the electrode potential moves to a more negative value. This is exactly what the Nernst equation predicts.

Final answer: Electrode potential becomes more negative (decreases) because decreased $[\text{Ni}^{2+}]$ shifts $\text{Ni}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ni(s)}$ to the left, favouring oxidation.

hints: Identify oxidised species as $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, reduced species as $\text{Cr}^{2+}$, and z as 1 for the change $\text{Cr}^{3+} + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cr}^{2+}$.
Set up the ratio $[\text{oxidised}]/[\text{reduced}] = 0.60/0.15$ before substituting into $E = E^{\ominus} + (0.059/z)\log$ ratio.
walkthrough:
Set up the Nernst terms correctly**
For $\text{Cr}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + e^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cr}^{2+}(\text{aq})$, $z = 1$ because one electron is transferred. Oxidised is $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, reduced is $\text{Cr}^{2+}$.
$$E = E^{\ominus} + \frac{0.059}{z}\log\frac{[\text{oxidised species}]}{[\text{reduced species}]}$$

Substitute and calculate**
Put in $E^{\ominus} = -0.41$ V and the concentrations:
$$E = -0.41 + \frac{0.059}{1}\log\frac{0.60}{0.15}$$
$$E = -0.41 + 0.059\log 4.0$$
$$E = -0.41 + 0.0355 = -0.37 \text{ V}$$
Because the ratio is greater than 1, log is positive, so E is slightly less negative than $E^{\ominus}$, which makes chemical sense as extra $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ favours reduction.
